sources.citation: Bullock, Juliann. 2015. The Sociolinguistic Situation in the Kaser Area. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2015-001. Dallas: SIL International. 73 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Appendix A p.34: 'in all three languages, negation can be indicated tonally' (Ikobi example karimao with two pitch patterns). Mouwase (Table 18, pp.51-56) and Barikewa (Table 19, pp.57-62) wordlists carry pitch diacritics and occasional stress ticks, with no key or discussion.

sources.citation: Usher, Timothy (with Robert Petterson). n.d. 'Kaser'. New Guinea World.
sources.note: Segmental phonology of Turama River Kaser (= Ikobi, ikob1240, sister language, not Omati) after Petterson 2011 ms; no suprasegmental section, no mention of stress or tone.

sources.citation: Usher, Timothy. n.d. 'Barikewa'. New Guinea World.
sources.note: 'There is no published phonology of Barikewa.' Only wordlists: Johnston 1921-22, Petterson 1991, Carr 2006.

sources.citation: Usher, Timothy. n.d. 'Mouwase'. New Guinea World.
sources.note: Phonology '[under construction]': 11 consonants, 5 vowels, no final consonants or clusters; nothing on stress or tone. Sources: Johnston 1919-20, Franklin 1973, Carr 2006, Petterson 2014 dictionary (1,198 terms).

sources.citation: Usher, Timothy. n.d. 'Omati River'. New Guinea World (Santa Fe Institute; hosted UZH).https://newguineaworld.linguistik.uzh.ch/families/papuan-gulf/kikori-river/rumu-omati-river/omati-river/start
sources.note: Family-level (proto-Omati River) reconstruction: 'Tone is contrastive, but has not been indicated in the protoforms below.' One Mouwase form -tuku 'elbow' raised 'probably because it is destressed in a compound'. No rule for stress placement. Cites unpublished Petterson 2011 (Kaser phonology, dictionary), 2014 (Mouwase dictionary, Kaser verbs), 1991 (Barikiwa list), Carr 2006.

sources.citation: Petterson, Robert G. 2014. Mouwase dictionary. Manuscript, SIL-PNG, Ukarumpa (1,198 entries; 'phonemic' forms per Usher).

sources.note: The only lexical/phonological record of Mouwase (= the larger half of 'Omati') by a linguist resident in the area; if any statement on Mouwase tone or stress exists it would be in its phonological preamble or in how headwords are marked.
